title: Paying wages
hookLine: pay the worker before his sweat dries (Ibn Majah)
tomorrow: someone owes you money and can't pay. now what?

cards: An invoice that says net thirty. A babysitter waiting by the door while the parents dig for cash. A first paycheck that arrives a week late, with a sorry email.
So when exactly is pay owed? A hadith in Ibn Majah gives an answer you can feel on your skin: give the worker his wages before his sweat dries.

teach.b: Muslims read that line in more than one way, and both readings have a case. The first stays close to the picture. Sweat dries fast.
Work done today is paid today, especially for the day laborer who needs it for dinner. Every hour you hold it, you're holding something that isn't yours.

teach.h: READING TWO: PAY IT WHEN DUE.
teach.b: The second reading hears it as a picture of promptness.

Pay can come weekly or monthly, if that's what both sides agreed; what the saying forbids is dragging past the day it's due. A business with a payroll date isn't breaking the hadith, so long as the date is kept.
Some scholars also note the line's chain is debated on its own, and lean on other reports beside it. And here is where the two agree, in a report in Sahih al-Bukhari.
God says there are three whom He will oppose on the Day of Resurrection, and one is a man who hires a worker, takes the full work from him, and doesn't pay his wage.
So the question isn't really weekly or daily. It's whether the worker has to chase what he's already earned. One to tell a friend: in that hadith, God Himself takes the unpaid worker's side.

how: Muslim employers are taught to pay wages in full and on time, whether by the day or on an agreed schedule; withholding a worker's earned pay is counted a serious wrong.

o: paying workers only when the business is doing well
giving workers their earned pay on time, in full
tipping a server on top of the price of a meal

games.q: the saying and the readings — tap the pairs.

s: in a report in Bukhari, God opposes one who hires a worker and withholds his wage
he takes the full work and doesn't pay: one of three God will oppose.
Muslims all agree the saying means pay within the hour
some read it close to the letter; others as 'on the agreed day'. both forbid holding back what's due.

games.q: your aunt hires a neighbor's teenager to rake leaves on Saturday, then says she'll pay with the family bills at month's end. they never agreed on that. what fits?
o: month's end is fine; the one paying decides when pay is due.
pay when the job is done, or on a day they both agree to first.
pay half now and half later, so everyone shares the wait.
games.why: both readings meet here: pay on completion, or on the day agreed. what neither allows is the worker waiting on terms they never accepted.

practice: Bring to mind anyone you owe right now: a friend who covered lunch, a sitter, a coworker who chipped in for a gift. Send it now, or write down the exact day you will.
Then sit for the rest of the time with nothing owed left floating.

wordCard.voice: Paying wages: giving a worker what they've earned, on time, without making them chase it. Before the sweat dries.

orig.note: Arabic: a wage, the pay for work done.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: before the sweat dries, the pay is theirs. Three of ten, done.

sources.ref: Sunan Ibn Majah 2443 (give the worker his wages before his sweat dries)
Sahih al-Bukhari 2227 (hadith qudsi: three whom God will oppose, including one who hires a worker, takes full work and doesn't pay him)
